name: Heraklion
title: Ship Thickness Measurement in Heraklion | UTM & Hull Gauging
description: UTM and hull gauging in Heraklion, Crete for ro-pax ferries, island tankers and cargo ships: lay-up refit readings, deck and tank thickness measurement.
h1: Heraklion, Crete: Ultrasonic Gauging for Ferries, Tankers and Cargo Ships
intro: Heraklion is the largest port on Crete and the island's lifeline: overnight ro-pax ferries from Piraeus, cruise ships, fuel tankers and general cargo all pass through its harbour. Ships are rarely idle here for long, so gauging has to be planned around the timetable. We send a team from India to the vessel, and the readings are taken during layovers, winter lay-up or a cargo stop, with the scope agreed beforehand.

highlights.p: Ro-pax ships on the Piraeus service spend short periods alongside, while the quieter winter months leave room for tank, void and vehicle deck readings that the summer timetable does not allow. We plan around both.

Crete depends on shipped fuel, bulk supplies and containers. The tankers and cargo ships serving it are often coastal or short-sea tonnage, where deck, hatch and ballast tank readings answer most superintendent questions.
A ferry in port for a few hours cannot be opened up on the day. We agree spaces, entry permits and gas-free certificates with the master in advance, so the team works from the first minute alongside.

port.h: Heraklion: the harbour that feeds Crete
p: Heraklion sits on the north coast of Crete, facing the Sea of Crete, and its harbour is protected by a long breakwater with the old Venetian fortress at the entrance. The port is the busiest on the island by passengers and by cargo, and it is run by the Heraklion Port Authority. Ferries arrive from Piraeus most evenings and sail again early the next day, and other services link Heraklion with Santorini and Dodecanese islands in the summer. Cruise ships anchor off or berth alongside depending on size and season, and the harbour fills with day visitors when they do.

Behind the passenger traffic sits the freight that keeps an island of several hundred thousand residents supplied. Container ships and ro-ro units bring consumer goods and building materials, general cargo ships deliver bulk supplies and agricultural inputs, and product tankers discharge fuel for the island's power generation, road transport and aviation. Much of this is carried by coastal or short-sea tonnage rather than ocean-going ships, and many vessels are older tonnage on regular Aegean and Mediterranean rotations. A ship in this pattern accumulates wear on weather decks, hatch covers, ballast tank boundaries and vehicle ramps.

The weather shapes the working year. In summer the northerly meltemi can build quickly across the Sea of Crete, making berthing and launch transfers awkward for a day or two at a time, while winter brings southwesterly swells and lower passenger numbers. That winter window is when owners schedule refits, and when thickness readings can be taken in spaces that are inaccessible during the busy season. Heraklion therefore sees two kinds of gauging demand: short targeted checks during ordinary port calls, and planned condition work on ships laid up or in a seasonal refit.

facilities.h: Where gauging can be done in and around Heraklion
p: Within the harbour, gauging is done alongside at the ferry and cargo quays, subject to the port authority's ISPS arrangements and the ship's agent. Cargo ships discharging bulk or general cargo offer open holds and hatch covers for a day or two, while product tankers at the fuel berths are limited to deck, deck piping and ballast tanks inside the terminal's permit rules. For ro-pax ferries the useful spaces are the vehicle decks, ramps, ballast tanks and voids, which are easiest to open when the ship is out of service.

Heraklion is not a major ship-repair centre and has no large drydock, so ships needing hull steel work normally go to the repair zones near Athens, or to yards elsewhere in the Aegean or the wider Mediterranean. That makes gauging here a preparation step. Readings taken during a Heraklion layover give the technical manager a measured picture to send to yards when requesting steel renewal quotations, and they let the docking be planned without surprises. Where a vessel is laid up in the harbour for the winter, a longer gauging programme is realistic.
list: Passenger and ferry quays — vehicle deck, ramp and ballast tank readings on ro-pax ships during layovers or winter lay-up
Cargo and container berths — hatch cover, coaming, hold and deck gauging on general cargo and container ships during discharge
Fuel berths — deck, deck piping and ballast tank gauging on product tankers, within the terminal's permit-to-work system
Cruise berths and anchorage — tank and void readings on cruise ships where the turnaround allows access
Winter lay-up berths — extended gauging of ships idle between seasons, planned with the owner's refit list

context.h: Port state control and island shipping rules
p: Greece belongs to the Paris MoU, and port state control inspections at Heraklion are carried out by the Hellenic Coast Guard, which also oversees the safety of the many passenger ships serving the islands. Ferries on domestic routes face frequent inspections and survey cycles tied to passenger certificates, so owners keep structural condition records closely. The Mediterranean emission control area for sulphur, in force from 1 May 2025, covers Cretan waters. EU ETS has covered shipping since 2024 and FuelEU Maritime since 2025, and both affect voyages between Piraeus and Crete.

For ships calling at EU ports, the Ship Recycling Regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board, and a sale or change of manager may prompt a fresh look at the hull as well as the paperwork. Island ferries carry passengers all year, so owners take steel wastage on vehicle decks and ballast tanks seriously and prefer to find it between seasons. Fuel and bulk shipping to Crete is often managed from Piraeus, which means a gauging decision taken in an Athens technical department may be carried out at Heraklion on the next suitable call.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Heraklion
jobs.p: Heraklion work usually starts with a question from a technical department: has a known area of wastage advanced, will a deck survive another season, or what steel should be budgeted for the next docking. We scope the job to fit the ship's schedule and the spaces that can be made safe, and report results by area so the superintendent can act on them before the ship sails.
list: Vehicle deck and ramp plating readings on a ro-pax ferry during winter lay-up, followed by ballast tank gauging to support the refit specification.
Hatch cover and coaming gauging on a general cargo ship discharging at the cargo quay before a new charter fixture.
Deck plating and deck piping readings on a coastal product tanker alongside the fuel berth, ahead of an oil-major vetting inspection.
Pre-docking gauging of ballast tanks and void spaces on an older container ship, giving the manager a steel estimate to send to Perama or other yards.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard piping check on a ro-pax ship after a weeping flange was reported by the engine room.

logistics: The team flies in to Heraklion's Nikos Kazantzakis Airport, usually connecting through Athens, and reaches the harbour by road within the city. Port passes under ISPS, access to the fuel berths and any launch boarding are arranged through the ship's agent, with crew lists, technician certificates and equipment lists sent beforehand. Greece is a Schengen state, so each technician needs a Schengen visa issued in India. Ferry schedules are fixed months ahead, so telling us the winter refit dates early lets the visa applications start well before the ship is available.

faqs.q: Can a ferry be gauged during its Heraklion layover?
faqs.a: To a limited extent. A ferry alongside for a few hours can usually accommodate deck, ramp and accessible plating readings, but tank entry needs the spaces ventilated, tested and certified in advance. For ballast tanks and voids, the winter lay-up is a far better window, and we agree a plan with the superintendent around that period.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Heraklion for steel renewal?
faqs.a: Not on the scale needed for major hull work. Ships needing steel renewal normally go to yards near Athens or elsewhere in the Mediterranean. That is why gauging at Heraklion is best used as preparation: measured readings let the owner compare yard offers and order plate before the ship leaves the island.

faqs.q: How does the meltemi affect work at Heraklion?
faqs.a: Strong northerly wind in summer can delay berthing, launch transfers and anchorage work for a day or two at a time. Gauging alongside inside the harbour is less affected, but tank preparation and shore access still follow the master's decisions. We leave slack in the schedule for summer jobs and keep the superintendent informed of any change.

faqs.q: Can product tankers be gauged at the fuel berth?
faqs.a: Yes, within the terminal's permit rules. Work at a fuel berth is usually limited to deck plating, deck piping and ballast tanks, and may be restricted during cargo transfer. The agent and the terminal confirm what is allowed, and we plan the readings to fit the discharge schedule rather than hold it up.

faqs.q: Can one trip cover Heraklion and Souda?
faqs.a: Often yes. Both are on the north coast of Crete and are linked by road, so a single mobilisation can cover ships at each if the dates line up. Give us the vessels and their expected windows, and we will plan the order of jobs, the visa period and the agent arrangements together.
